title: Foie Gras Farm Conversion
scenario: Fourth-generation duck farmer Étienne Marchand in southwest France learns that a new regional rule will tighten welfare standards on force-feeding, making his small farm uneconomical. A neighbouring cooperative offers to buy his birds and land, while an animal welfare charity offers a grant to convert to free-range egg production at lower income. Étienne's family and the village's identity are tied to the product, but he has long felt uneasy about the practice. A buyer wants an answer within a month.
options: Sell to the cooperative, which will continue the practice under the new rules, and secure his family's finances.
Convert to free-range eggs with the charity grant, ending a family tradition and accepting a lower income.
Continue operating under the tighter standards, gambling that regulations will remain manageable.

title: Dog Meat Festival Permit
scenario: District administrator Park Soo-jin in South Korea must decide whether to renew a permit for a seasonal market where a small number of dogs are still sold for meat. Elderly vendors say it is a lawful tradition and their last income, while younger residents and an animal charity find it cruel. The national position is ambiguous. A decision denying the permit would likely be litigated, and renewal would draw protests. She has two weeks.
options: Deny the permit, prioritising the welfare of the dogs and the shift in public values.
Renew the permit with strict welfare conditions, respecting vendors' livelihoods and the lawful status of the practice.
Renew once with a binding wind-down date and transition support for the vendors, a compromise that satisfies neither side fully.

title: Primate Study on a Dementia Cure
scenario: Lead researcher Dr. Valentina Cruz at a Brazilian university is planning an experiment on thirty macaques to test a promising gene therapy for early-onset dementia. The trial may take years off the development of a treatment affecting thousands of families. The animals would undergo surgery and long-term monitoring with some suffering. Alternative organoid models exist but are less predictive. The ethics board seeks her justification before approving.
options: Proceed with the macaque study, judging that human benefit and the study's predictive value justify the animals' suffering.
Use organoid models only, accepting slower and less certain progress to avoid primate suffering.
Run the macaque study with a smaller group of ten animals, risking that the results are inconclusive.

title: The Retired Racehorse
scenario: Horse trainer Declan O'Rourke in Australia has a champion gelding with a career-ending leg injury. Surgery could allow a comfortable life as a companion horse but costs more than he can afford, and the owner will only pay for euthanasia. The horse has no insurance value and is not yet in pain at rest. A sanctuary has offered a place if Declan can fund the surgery and transport himself, which would take most of his savings.
options: Euthanise the horse as the owner wishes, sparing further cost and any uncertain recovery.
Pay for the surgery and sanctuary from his own savings, giving the horse a chance at a long life.
Seek crowd-funding for the surgery for two weeks, keeping the horse in managed discomfort while he raises funds.

title: Octopus on the Menu
scenario: Restaurateur Sofia Papadaki in Crete has built her reputation on grilled octopus caught by local fishers. After reading research on octopus intelligence and the pain responses of cephalopods, she questions whether to keep it on the menu. It accounts for a third of her sales, and her suppliers are small family boats. Removing it could cost jobs among her ten staff and fishers. She is finalising next season's menu.
options: Remove octopus from the menu, acting on concerns about sentience even at a financial cost.
Keep octopus but source only from fishers who use quick humane killing methods, accepting some remaining ethical doubt.
Keep octopus unchanged, judging the evidence uncertain and weighing livelihoods and local food culture heavily.
tension: emerging evidence of sentience vs. livelihoods

title: Battery Hens and the Power Cut
scenario: Poultry farmer Chidi Eze in Nigeria houses 5,000 hens in cages when a power outage disables his ventilation fans on a day of extreme heat. Without action, many birds will die within hours. He can open the cage doors and move birds into the yard shade, risking predators and chaos and weakening his flock's laying schedule, or sell a large number immediately to a processor at a low price. He has minutes to decide.
options: Open the cages and let hens into the shaded yard, saving as many as possible despite the risks and disruption.
Sell a large part of the flock immediately for slaughter, avoiding a mass heat death but ending their lives.
Rig emergency water-spraying with buckets and neighbours' help, trying to save the whole flock at risk of failing.

title: Bullfight Heritage Subsidy
scenario: Municipal culture officer Alejandro Ruiz in Colombia faces a vote on whether to continue public funding for the town's annual bullring festival. The festival draws visitors, supports artisans and small hotels, and is cherished by older residents. An animal welfare movement, including many young residents, argues that public money should not support the killing of bulls. A referendum is not on offer, so his recommendation will probably decide the matter.
options: Recommend ending public funding, aligning public money with the welfare of the animals and changing community values.
Recommend continuing the subsidy, respecting the festival's cultural meaning and the livelihoods around it.
Recommend redirecting the subsidy toward a festival without bull killing, hoping to retain visitors but risking alienation of its supporters.

title: Rats in the Seed Library
scenario: Coordinator Hannah Weiss manages a community seed library and garden in a Berlin housing block. Rats have started raiding stored seeds, and the housing association is pushing her to use poison or lose the space. Poison risks harming foxes and urban hedgehogs that visit, and stray cats the residents feed. Traps are slower and sometimes cruel, and sealing storage would cost more than the library can afford. She has one week to respond to the housing association.
options: Use poison bait stations to save the seed collection quickly, accepting a risk to other animals.
Use snap traps and costly rodent-proof storage funded by donations, accepting delay and a risk to the library.
Move the seeds off-site and let the rats remain, giving up part of the garden's mission and the community's convenience.
tension: protecting the collection vs. harm to other animals

title: A Vet's Choice at the Herders' Camp
scenario: Veterinarian Dr. Batbayar Ganzorig in Mongolia is called by herders after a harsh winter 'dzud'. Thousands of animals are starving, and he has limited feed and medicine. He can concentrate resources on breeding females to preserve the herd's future, treat the most visibly suffering animals, or advise herders to slaughter weaker livestock early to avoid prolonged starvation and obtain meat. Families' survival depends on the herds.
options: Focus resources on breeding females, sacrificing weaker animals to protect the herd's recovery and the families' future.
Treat the most visibly suffering animals first, prioritising relief of pain over the herd's economic recovery.
Advise early slaughter of the weakest animals, easing their suffering and securing food at the cost of the herd's size.

title: Dolphin Show Closure
scenario: Park manager Wei Lin in China oversees an aquarium whose dolphin show provides most of the revenue for the entire park and its 140 staff. Marine biologists and activists say the dolphins' small tanks harm their well-being and shortened life spans. A sea sanctuary offers to take the dolphins but would need two years and half a million dollars, and release into the wild is not possible. Wei must propose a plan to the owners.
options: Close the show and fund the transfer to the sanctuary, accepting job losses and cuts across the park.
Continue the show while upgrading tanks and reducing performances, partially addressing welfare concerns.
Phase out the show over two years while seeking sponsorship for the sanctuary move, a gradual approach that leaves the dolphins in tanks for now.

title: Free-Range Eggs for the Food Bank
scenario: Food bank director Marguerite Delacroix in Quebec is offered a large donation of eggs at no cost, but the producer uses caged hens. The food bank's clients, many of them children, rely heavily on donated protein, and egg supplies have been low. Several volunteers object that accepting the eggs supports an industry they consider cruel, and some donors give specifically to the food bank because of its ethical sourcing reputation. A truck is arriving tomorrow.
options: Accept the donation, prioritising the nutrition of clients who have few alternatives.
Decline the donation, upholding the food bank's ethical sourcing commitments even though supplies are short.
Accept this single shipment while launching a campaign to secure higher-welfare eggs in future, which may not succeed.

title: Insect Protein Plant Welfare Rules
scenario: Startup founder Joaquim Pinto in Portugal is building a plant to farm black soldier fly larvae as animal feed and human food. Evidence on insect sentience is uncertain, but some studies suggest larvae may feel noxious stimuli. Killing by freezing is cheaper, while slower, costlier methods may reduce possible suffering. The business promises lower land and emissions footprints than soy. His investors are indifferent to the question, and he alone chooses the process.
options: Adopt the cheaper freezing method, relying on the uncertain evidence and the environmental benefit of the product.
Invest in the costlier rapid method, giving the benefit of the doubt to larvae at higher cost and lower margin.
Delay production while commissioning independent welfare research, risking funding and competitors' advantage.
tension: precaution under uncertainty vs. environmental benefit

title: A Pig Farm and the Next Pandemic
scenario: Chief veterinary officer Dr. Nguyen Thi Lan in Vietnam learns that African swine fever has appeared at a smallholder farm, and her protocol requires culling all pigs within three kilometres. That affects 400 families, many of whom lose their only savings, and compensation is limited. Allowing a quarantine without culling risks wider spread across the country's pig herd and food supply. She must give the order tonight.
options: Order the full cull within the radius, prioritising the containment of the disease and the nation's herd.
Order a partial cull of confirmed and highest-risk farms with quarantine, reducing losses but risking spread.
Order the cull but delay execution for 48 hours to arrange compensation, risking further transmission.
tension: public health and food security vs. household losses
certainty of harm vs. uncertain risk

title: Reindeer Games and Zoo Breeding
scenario: Zoo director Annika Haugen in Norway oversees breeding of a rare species of mountain goat held in her zoo. A newborn has a defect that would require ongoing care and prevent breeding. Culling surplus animals is standard practice in the breeding programme, but school visitors and staff are attached to the kid. A private donor will pay for lifelong care in a sanctuary but not for the cost of transport. The programme coordinator needs a decision this week.
options: Euthanise the kid in line with the programme's policy, preserving space and resources for breeding animals.
Accept the donor's offer and transfer the kid, accepting extra cost and a departure from the programme's policy.
Keep the kid in the zoo as an education animal, accepting that other conservation work will get fewer resources.
tension: conservation programme rules vs. individual animal

title: Wet Market Reform Without Shutting Livelihoods
scenario: Municipal health chief Dr. Kofi Asante in Ghana is considering banning live animal sales at the city's central market after an outbreak of avian flu in the region. Hundreds of traders, mostly women, sell live poultry and cannot afford refrigeration. Customers also prefer fresh-killed birds for cultural and cost reasons. A ban would reduce zoonotic risk and animal suffering in crowded cages but may push trade into unregulated roadside sales.
options: Ban live sales in the central market, prioritising health risk and animal conditions even if trade moves elsewhere.
Allow live sales with new cage, hygiene and slaughter rules, accepting some remaining disease and welfare risk.
Ban live sales only during outbreak alerts, which protects livelihoods most of the year but permits periodic risk.
tension: public health and animal welfare vs. traders' livelihoods

title: Guide Dog Puppy Washout
scenario: Puppy raiser Marta Kowalczyk in Poland has spent fourteen months training a labrador for a guide dog charity. The dog has failed final assessment due to anxiety around traffic. The charity's policy is to rehome failed dogs as pets, but the waiting list is long and the dog is bonded to Marta, who cannot afford to keep it long term. A blind applicant has offered to take a trained dog, even one that is imperfect, since the wait for others is two years.
options: Give the dog to the blind applicant despite its anxiety, honouring the applicant's need and willingness to try.
Keep the dog herself, prioritising the animal's wellbeing and the bond formed over the applicant's request.
Follow the charity's policy and rehome the dog as a pet, ensuring safety for both dog and any would-be handler.

title: A Sacrificial Festival and the New Law
scenario: Temple priest Ramesh Thapa in Nepal leads a community that has practised an annual animal sacrifice for centuries. A new court ruling bans the practice, citing animal cruelty, though enforcement is patchy. Some devotees will continue in secret, which would make the animals' deaths less supervised, and others say they will abstain. Ramesh must decide how his temple handles this year's festival, with several thousand worshippers expected and police watching.
options: Comply with the ruling fully, replacing sacrifice with symbolic offerings and risking splits within the community.
Continue the sacrifice with veterinary supervision and humane methods, defying the ruling to preserve a sacred practice.
Hold the festival without sacrifice at the temple but leave individuals to decide privately, a position that avoids confrontation but not the practice.
tension: religious tradition vs. animal welfare law

title: Lab Mice and the Lab Closure
scenario: Lab technician Samuel Adeyinka in South Africa discovers that a university department is closing and will euthanise 600 breeding mice. A sanctuary could take around a hundred, and a nearby lab could take others, but none of the mice are suitable for pet homes and some carry health issues. Samuel can quietly smuggle some out, push the department to wait, or comply with procedure. The deadline is Friday.
options: Comply with the protocol, trusting the department's judgement and avoiding misconduct.
Arrange legitimate transfer of the healthier mice to the sanctuary and the other lab, delaying the closure schedule.
Remove a number of mice without permission to save as many as possible, risking his job and the department's reputation.

title: The Fox in the Henhouse Law
scenario: Rural councillor Eilidh MacLeod in the Scottish Highlands votes on a request from crofters to allow night shooting of foxes using thermal scopes during lambing season. Fox predation causes significant losses for small crofts, while conservationists say foxes also control rabbits and that non-lethal fencing and guardian animals work. A refusal may make crofters resort to illegal snaring. The vote is tied until hers is cast.
options: Vote to allow the shooting under licence, protecting crofters' livelihoods and the lambs.
Vote against, requiring non-lethal methods first and funding fencing grants, accepting lambing losses.
Vote for a one-year trial with mandatory reporting, an arrangement that may satisfy neither side.

title: Circus Elephants Retirement
scenario: Circus owner Raj Malhotra in India has three ageing elephants who can no longer perform. A government sanctuary offers a place but under conditions that Raj fears will lead to poor care as it is overcrowded. A private buyer would use them for tourist rides. Keeping them costs more than the family business can bear, and the family's older members consider the elephants part of the family. Raj has to choose before the licence lapses.
options: Send the elephants to the government sanctuary, accepting its flaws as the lawful and non-commercial option.
Sell them to the tourist operator, receiving funds to support the circus workers but exposing the elephants to ongoing work.
Keep the elephants and seek donations for private care, risking the family's finances and the animals' wellbeing.
tension: legal option vs. better care elsewhere

title: Sheep Transport by Sea
scenario: Port veterinarian Dr. Karim Haddad in Jordan inspects a livestock ship carrying 20,000 sheep from Australia that has been delayed by heat and mechanical trouble. Mortality on board is rising. Refusing to unload risks more deaths at sea, while unloading into overcrowded holding pens could spread disease to local flocks. The importer says Eid demand makes quick sale essential. The shipping agent presses him for a ruling within the hour.
options: Order immediate unloading with quarantine, prioritising the survival of the animals on board.
Refuse unloading until disease testing is done, protecting local flocks while risking more deaths at sea.
Unload a portion of the healthiest animals and keep others aboard while testing proceeds, a split solution with uncertain outcomes.
tension: suffering animals vs. local herd health

title: Wild Honey and the Hive's Share
scenario: Beekeeper Tomasz Wieczorek in Slovenia notices that a harsh summer has left his hives with small stores. Selling honey as usual would fund his family's winter needs, but taking it means feeding bees sugar syrup, which is less healthy and risks colony loss. His customers expect local honey and he has pre-orders. A rival beekeeper has advised him to harvest and feed sugar syrup, as most do. He must decide before the first frost.
options: Harvest as usual and feed sugar syrup, as is common practice and keeps his income stable.
Leave most of the honey in the hives, accepting lost income to protect the bees' health.
Harvest only the surplus from the strongest hives and refund some customers, balancing both concerns imperfectly.

title: Rescued Greyhounds and the Track
scenario: Racing club secretary Mick Doherty in Ireland learns that his track's finances depend on greyhound racing, which supports forty jobs and the village pub scene. Injury rates are high, and each season dozens of dogs are retired, with rehoming spaces limited. A campaign group has offered to help fund rehoming only if the club agrees to a phase-out of racing within five years. The club's committee will vote on the proposal.
options: Support the phase-out agreement, ending racing in exchange for rehoming help and a reduced injury toll over time.
Oppose it, protecting local jobs and the sport while promising to improve safety and rehoming without outside conditions.
Propose a reduced race schedule with safer track surfaces and a rehoming guarantee, an uneasy compromise.

title: Camel Racing Child Jockeys' Robots
scenario: Racing federation official Khalid Al-Mansoori in the UAE is considering a proposal to require camels to be fitted with specialised racing equipment and training schedules that increase their speed. Animal welfare experts warn it will cause chronic strain, while breeders point out that camels are worth enormous sums and are well cared for. Banning the measures would reduce the sport's prestige and sponsorship. Khalid must present a regulation draft to the federation.
options: Adopt the equipment and schedules, trusting breeders' care and valuing the sport's competitiveness.
Prohibit them and introduce veterinary monitoring, protecting the camels at the cost of prestige and sponsorship.
Allow the equipment with annual veterinary approval and independent inspections, risking weak enforcement.

title: The Last Wild Horses and the Ranchers
scenario: Land manager Dolores Whitehorse in Nevada oversees a rangeland where a herd of wild horses has grown beyond the carrying capacity, causing erosion and competing with cattle and native deer. Her options include a costly fertility control programme, a roundup and adoption programme that stresses the horses, or allowing ranchers to reduce herd size through culling. Public opinion is strongly in favour of the horses, while ranchers face drought-related losses.
options: Roll out fertility control across the herd, accepting slow results and continued range damage in the short term.
Conduct a roundup and adoption programme, reducing numbers quickly but stressing the horses and risking unadopted animals.
Permit limited culling alongside fertility control, protecting range quality and ranchers but provoking public anger.
tension: animal life vs. range ecology and ranchers
